chapter_summary.text: This chapter teaches how to measure angles with a protractor, how to use the properties of vertical angles, straight‑line angles and angles around a point, and how to find unknown angles using these ideas.

learning_objectives.text: Measure an angle using a protractor.
Identify and use vertically opposite angles.
Apply the rule that angles on a straight line add to $180^\circ$.
Apply the rule that angles at a point add to $360^\circ$.
Calculate unknown angles by subtraction from $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$ or $360^\circ$.

meaning.text: The space between two lines that meet at a point, measured in degrees.
A tool used to measure the size of an angle.
Two angles that are opposite each other when two lines cross; they are equal.
Angles that lie on the same line; together they total $180^\circ$.
Angles that share a common vertex; together they total $360^\circ$.

explanation.text: The book shows how to line up the base of a protractor with one side of the angle, read the degree marking where the other side meets the scale, and record the measurement. It also shows using a compass‑rose to work out turns between directions.

The book explains that vertically opposite angles are equal, that the angles on a straight line add to $180^\circ$, and that the angles around a point add to $360^\circ$. Unknown angles are found by subtracting the known angles from these totals.
A right angle is $90^\circ$. Removing the given $42^\circ$ leaves $48^\circ$ for the unknown angle.
Angles on a straight line total $180^\circ$. Taking away $37^\circ$ leaves $143^\circ$.
A full turn is $360^\circ$. Removing $15^\circ$ gives the remaining angle $345^\circ$.
Each main direction is $90^\circ$ apart. South‑East is halfway between South ($180^\circ$) and East ($90^\circ$), so it is $135^\circ$ from North. West to South‑West is a $45^\circ$ turn.

worked_examples.title: Finding an angle on a straight line (DBE)

explanation.text: Angles on a straight line add to $180^\circ$. Subtract the two given angles to get the remaining angle.

worked_examples.title: Finding an angle at a point (x)

explanation.text: All angles around a point total $360^\circ$. Remove the three known angles to leave $35^\circ$.
A straight line through O gives $180^\circ$. Subtract the two adjacent angles to get the remaining angle.

misconception.text: Thinking that the angles on a straight line add to $360^\circ$.

correction.text: Angles on a straight line always add to $180^\circ$.

misconception.text: Assuming vertically opposite angles are different.

correction.text: Vertically opposite angles are always equal.

question.text: What angle do you turn through when you start facing north and turn clockwise to south‑east?
What angle do you turn through when you start facing west and turn counter‑clockwise to south‑west?
If you start facing north‑west and turn clockwise $90^\circ$, which direction are you now facing?
After turning counter‑clockwise $225^\circ$ you end up facing east. Which direction were you facing at the start?
Find the unknown angle $\angle p$ in a right‑angle diagram where the other angle is $42^\circ$.
Find the unknown angle $\angle q$ in a straight‑line diagram where the other angle is $37^\circ$.
Find the unknown angle $\angle r$ when it is a full rotation minus $15^\circ$.
In the figure where $\angle w = 46^\circ$, what is $\angle x$ (the vertically opposite angle)?
In the figure with $\angle AOC = 105^\circ$ and $\angle COD = 50^\circ$, find $\angle COB$.
Calculate $\angle DBE$ given $\angle ABD = 35^\circ$ and $\angle EBC = 55^\circ$.
Find $\angle x$ in the diagram where the other angles are $90^\circ$, $80^\circ$ and $155^\circ$.

review_checklist.text: I can measure an angle with a protractor.
I can identify vertically opposite angles and state that they are equal.
I can use the $180^\circ$ rule for angles on a straight line.
I can use the $360^\circ$ rule for angles around a point.
I can find an unknown angle by subtracting known angles from $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$ or $360^\circ$.
